The high-voltage dummy-load tests of the ITER PF1-1 and PF6-1 converter units ran on 28 September and 12–13 October 2026. The slow archive holds only 2 s indications of them. The waveforms were captured on a stand-alone HIOKI U8975 recorder wired from the LCC terminals, outside UDA and DAN. The recorder files are expected from the commissioning team in the week of 19 October 2026 (dummy-load evidence, sections 7 and 8). They will be the first measured switching waveforms of an ITER coil converter.

This plan makes those files a test rather than a calibration. The JT-60SA work showed how much that matters. The 2021-fitted booster model failed its pre-registered line criteria on all six held-out 2021 cases and all eight judged 2023 cases (booster-converter-model §5, filter-grounding-prediction §4). Only because the criteria were frozen first is that failure a measurement of the method's error, not a fit that hides it. The same JT-60SA replay located the error. On the same windows, the frequency-domain model under-predicts the 12f and 18f lines by 4–12 dB and the switched model over-predicts them by 2–10 dB. The two forms differ in how a converter commutates under load, not in the coupled plant (jt60sa-switched-pulse-replay §8–§10).

A dummy load has no coupled plant: 6.73 mH and a measured loop of about 5.5 mΩ. The recorder sees each bridge's current and voltage. The dummy-load files are therefore the cleanest available test of the one representation the ITER ripple results rest on, the loaded converter. Both of this repository's converter forms are frozen against them before the files are opened.

This plan supersedes iter-power-supply-model §5 and §6, which were written for the UDA slow archive, where §4 found no waveform. The converter identification of that §6 moves to §5 here, unchanged in method, on data that can carry it.

§1 — What the recorder files must carry, asked for now

The evidence page's section 8 already asks the commissioning team for the files, the recorder's sample rate, anti-alias filter, trigger, clock source and format, whether CU4 was recorded, and the T1–T4 loop-resistance paths. This section adds what the JT-60SA work found a ripple measurement cannot be scored without. It sends the combined list before the files arrive, so that a missing item is asked for once, not discovered later.

  • A source-off window on each recorded session: the converter blocked with the recorder live. Deblocked at zero reference is a different state, and it still produces ripple. Without this window no line can be told from pickup (jt60sa-coil-circuit-model §12).
  • How each voltage tap is wired: across the bridge or unit, or each terminal to ground. Record the ground return of the dummy-load circuit too, including the GVANCX ground-current monitor. An undocumented tap path is the one candidate JT-60SA could not exclude for its unexplained 12f coupling.
  • Channel scaling and sign for every probe, with the probe model, and the clock offset between the recorder and the slow archive.
  • The operating sequence keyed to recorder time: the preset current reference that Mini-CODAC sent, the selector code and the converter state. Ask for the inverting discharge ramps too, if any were run. The slow-archive runs stayed rectifying: 43 of 1,796 PF1 samples and 245 of 5,022 PF6 samples sit on the inverting side. A discharge at −80 kA/s or faster is the only way this load exercises inversion.

The deliverable is the request text, added as a subsection of section 8 of docs/evidence/iter-pf-dummy-load-tests.html. The lead sends it. A node never contacts the commissioning team. Done when that subsection lists every item above with the document it rests on, and the lead has recorded the date it was sent.

§2 — The blind prediction, frozen before the files are opened

Predict, from design values alone, what the recorder will show at the operating points the slow archive records. The circuit is one PF converter unit as the tests ran it: four six-pulse bridges, with C1 and C3 parallel on the positive polarity and C2 and C4 on the negative. It is fed from the Stage 1 PF transformer and AC busbar with stage1_pf_budget's commutation range (src/power_convertor/commutation.py). It drives the 6.73 mH ±1 % dummy load through the measured loop: T1 at 5.51 mΩ for PF1 and 5.43 mΩ for PF6. The circuit is built twice:

  • switched: ConverterNetwork.add_pf_unit with its FiringGenerator and the documented bridge bands, solved by power_convertor.switched_circuit;
  • analytic: the source form in power_convertor.bridge (BridgeSet, CirculatingBridgeGroup), as the whole-pulse ripple study uses it.

The operating points come from the 30 high-current runs of the slow-archive pulse table. Use each run's flat-top current and the measured angle of its conducting bridge pair. The firing-angle offset input is the evidence page's comparison of those angles with the design law on the dummy-load line (operating point): a median of −3.4° for PF1 and −3.0° for PF6 over |I| > 20 kA, with p10/p90 of −8.8°/+2.5° and −8.2°/+2.5°, which the band carries. The offset profile of scripts/iter/dummy_load_dc_regression.py, with shallow minima near +0.5° and +1.5°, is a conditional fit range that trades against transformer ratio, timing and bridge sharing. It is not an angle calibration and is not an input. Read the operating points and the offset from their owners rather than deriving them again: the points through load_samples and mode_counts in scripts/iter/dummy_load_dc_regression.py, over the session tables of scripts/iter/uda/dummy_load_sessions.py and dummy_load_windows.py, and the offset through law_offset and summary in scripts/figures/iter_dummy_load_operating_point.py. Import them, or extend them where the prediction needs a field they do not return, so that §4 scores against the same points. At each point, and over the circulating and one-bridge bands below 22 kA, predict:

  • each bridge's current, its share against its parallel partner, and the circulating current;
  • each bridge's voltage, with the commutation notch depth and overlap angle;
  • the unit's terminal-voltage lines at 300, 600, 900 and 1,200 Hz, in amplitude and phase relative to the AC supply;
  • the DC mean voltage against angle and current, the DC regulation curve that sets Xc;
  • the load-current ripple at 600 Hz;
  • the current at which the unit changes from one bridge to two. The design band puts it at 22 kA, 40 % of 55 kA. On the evidence page, the load-line model's constant-rate ramp lines step by about 2° at 17 kA, where one bridge starts to carry what two shared. The slow archive shows no single threshold shared by both units: at 20–30 kA PF1 has two same-polarity bridges in all 15 matched instants, while PF6 has one in 12 and two in 17. The prediction states which threshold it expects and why.

Each prediction carries a band from the propagated input ranges: the commutation budget, the load tolerance, the loop resistance from T1 to T4, and the firing-angle offset. The predictions are written to docs/figures/iter-dummy-load-prediction/prediction.json, stamped by power_convertor.provenance.revision, and recorded in docs/research/iter-dummy-load-prediction.html. The record names the tolerance chosen under decision prediction-tolerance and the operating points to be judged. The caller is scripts/iter/dummy_load_prediction.py.

Done when the record and the JSON are merged and their commit is written into this section's close note, before any recorder file is placed in the data directory. Two controls are stated in the record. Positive: at a 90° firing angle with the overlap set to zero, both forms reproduce the textbook six-pulse notch area and the 600 Hz line of an ideal twelve-pulse pair within 1 %. Negative: the unit built as an in-phase six-pulse pair, phase shift 0° rather than 30°, predicts 300 Hz lines in the two-bridge band at least 20 dB above the frozen unit's. The scoring section judges that negative arm against the measurement too.

§3 — Reading the recorder files

A reader for the HIOKI files in src/power_convertor/recorder_files.py. Its first form is built on a synthetic file the node writes in a stand-in layout: the recorder family's CSV text export, with a header of channel names, units, sampling interval and trigger time. No held document states the file format (the evidence page's section 7 says so), so the module states the layout as an assumption, refuses any other, and is reconciled with the real format when §1's request is answered. It returns each channel as time and value in SI units, in the contract signals.load and signals.units already return, with its sampling rate, scaling and sign stated, and refuses a channel it cannot scale. Channel signs follow the policy channel_sign.py owns. It is a new module because the HIOKI export is a format nothing in the repository reads; one public reader function is the whole surface it adds, and nothing is retired. The files themselves go to /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/power_convertor/data/iter/dummy-load-fast/, an absolute path, because data/ is ignored in a worktree.

Three checks decide what the files can say. This section builds them into the reader and proves them on the synthetic file. They are run on the first held recorder file as the first step of §4, behind gate g-idlv-1, and each is recorded in the evidence page under a new section on the recorder data.

  • Calibration: the recorder's current, averaged to the slow archive's samples, agrees with the archive's bridge-current indication within 2 % over every flat top. A channel that fails is not used for ripple.
  • Resolution: each characteristic line is marked resolved or aliased against the recorder's sampling rate and anti-alias filter, never against the slow archive's cadence.
  • Origin: in the source-off window no characteristic line rises more than 6 dB above the off-frequency noise floor. Without a source-off window, each line's origin is recorded as unresolved, and §4 judges it on that footing.

Done when the synthetic file reads through the reader and each of the three checks gives its verdict on a synthetic channel built to pass it and on one built to fail it. A unit test pins the synthetic file's scaled values. The test also shows the reader refusing a channel whose scaling is missing, and turns red when the refusal is removed. Reading a held recorder file is §4's first step, not this section's.

§4 — Scoring the frozen prediction

Score each quantity of §2 at each judged operating point against the recorder, with the line measures in power_convertor.signals and power_convertor.measurement. Pass the recorder's acquisition settings to them explicitly, never the JT-60SA defaults. The tolerance is the one frozen in §2. Each form, switched and analytic, gets its own verdict, and so does the in-phase negative arm. Every miss beyond tolerance is attributed: to an input range, to the converter representation, to the measurement, or left unresolved with the deciding measurement named, as filter-grounding-prediction §5 did.

The held files carry one DC current channel and one DC voltage channel per unit. No bridge current is recorded, so §2's per-bridge quantities have no channel: each bridge's current, its share against its parallel partner and the circulating current. Each of these gets the verdict not measurable from the held channels, with the missing channel named. Never infer a per-bridge value from the unit total. The notch depth and the overlap angle get the same verdict wherever the file's sampling cannot resolve them. A recorder file is paired with a frozen operating point by its current profile, matched against the slow archive in §3's calibration check, and not by its trigger date. The PF1 file's own trigger date reads 25 September, three days before the 28 September PF1-1 session whose operating points §2 froze. A file whose profile matches no frozen operating point is unpaired and is not scored, and the record says which file and why.

The record is a new section of docs/research/iter-dummy-load-prediction.html. It never rewrites the frozen predictions above it. Its figures go in docs/figures/iter-dummy-load-prediction/: measured against predicted line amplitude by operating point, one panel per unit, with the band, and the measured DC voltage ripple spectrum beside both forms, with the aliased lines marked where they land.

Done when §3's three checks are recorded against the held recorder file before any score is computed. Every judged operating point of a paired file needs a verdict for each form: a score, or not measurable with the missing channel named. Each miss must be attributed. The record must also say which form the ITER whole-pulse and switched studies should carry, and by how many decibels at 600 Hz. The negative arm must fail its 300 Hz lines. If it passes, the recorder cannot tell a twelve-pulse unit from a six-pulse pair, and the scoring is void.

§5 — The converter identified from the recorder, and carried into the ITER model

The method is the one iter-power-supply-model §6 wrote. It now runs on data that resolves the lines. Before any fit, commit the split, the tolerance and the held-out runs to docs/research/iter-pf-converter-fit.html. Then identify the line voltage and commutation reactance from the measured DC regulation, and from the overlap angle where the file's sampling resolves it. The parallel-bridge sharing impedance needs the bridge currents, which the held files do not record, so the record states that it is not identified from them. Call fit_base_supply (src/power_convertor/supply.py) with the recorder's sampling rate, phase shift and scored orders. It already takes all three: sample_rate (default FS_JT60SA, 4 kHz), a phase shift through base_configuration, and orders. Extend it only for a parameter the recorder needs that it does not take, keeping its defaults so the JT-60SA callers are unchanged. Its guard refuses a sampling rate at or below twice the highest fitted line, and its default orders (12f and 24f) would refuse both held files. So the orders are set per file. PF6, at 2 kHz, carries orders 6, 12 and 18 (300, 600 and 900 Hz). PF1, at 1 kHz, could carry order 6 alone, but its 300 Hz landing is shared with other folded lines under the reader's alias map, so PF1 enters the identification through its DC regulation only. The guard assumes a filtered input, and the recorder's filter was off. The fit therefore uses only the landings the reader marks resolved, and the negative control is scored on PF6. Pass the recorder's acquisition settings for the other two JT-60SA defaults as well, as the scoring tests already do: timing_skew_s=0, because the HIOKI recorder has no interleave skew, and a bandwidth_hz far above the highest fitted line, because with its filter off the recorder applies no low-pass in the fitted band. Never use the 104.57 µs skew or the 10 kHz bandwidth. The caller is a new scripts/iter/identify_pf_converter.py with its test tests/test_identify_pf_converter.py. It reads the reader's settings files under /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/power_convertor/data/iter/dummy-load-fast/derived/ and §4's scoring record, and nothing in iter-power-supply-model §6, which is deferred, is assumed to exist. Write the identified values to docs/figures/iter-pf-converter-fit/parameters.json.

Each identified value is set beside its IDM design value in the IDM register as a measured deviation. Decision as-built-values settles which value the integrated model then carries. Where the Xc range that keeps the held-out lines in tolerance spans more than a factor of two, the record states that those points do not identify Xc. It does not report a fitted value there.

Done when the held-out verdict is recorded and the negative control misses the held-out lines by more than the tolerance: the in-phase six-pulse pair, scored on 6f and 18f. The ITER studies whose converter inputs moved must be listed with the size of the move, so the integrated model's owner can rerun them.

§1 and §2 start together today. §2 needs decision prediction-tolerance locked before its record is written, and its merge must precede the arrival of the recorder files: a file read before the freeze makes §4 a fit, not a test. §3 can be built on a synthetic file meanwhile. §4 and §5 wait on gate g-idlv-1.

/reckon-build iter-dummy-load-validation §1

When it lands, score §4 from that settings file, with per-bridge quantities recorded as not measurable from the held channels. §5 follows §4.

/reckon-build iter-dummy-load-validation §4

iter-pf-dummy-load-tests

Evidence

§ Decisions

What tolerance is pre-registered for the dummy-load prediction?

JT-60SA judged its lines at ±3 dB. There the 6f and 12f lines landed within about 3 dB, while 18f and above missed by 10–13 dB.

The lead chose the band JT-60SA was judged at: within 3 dB on lines whose SNR is at least 10 dB, within 5 percent on the DC mean voltage and within 20 percent on the overlap angle. That makes the ITER dummy-load verdict directly comparable with the JT-60SA verdicts, where 6f and 12f landed within about 3 dB and 18f and above missed by 10-13 dB. A tighter band would likely fail on the input ranges alone, and a per-order band would excuse in advance the orders that failed at JT-60SA.

When the recorder identifies a converter parameter that differs from its IDM value, which value does the integrated ITER model carry?

IDM is the design authority, and DINA is never fitted to. A commissioning measurement of the installed converter is evidence about the machine as built, which is neither.

The lead chose the measured value. A commissioning recording of the installed converter is evidence about the machine as built, not a model to fit to the way DINA is. Where the recorder identifies a parameter, such as the commutation reactance or the parallel-bridge sharing impedance, beyond its held-out tolerance, the integrated model carries the measured value. The IDM design value is reported beside every affected result, and the deviation goes into the IDM register. Parameters the recorder does not identify keep their IDM values, and DINA's values are never used for any of them.
